newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung listens on rights, but blasted as deaf.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung listens on rights, but blasted as deaf.

text.p: Hong Kong's incoming leader backpedalled slightly on Thursday over proposed curbs on civil rights after the territory reverts to China on July 1, but pro-democracy politicians blasted the future government as deaf to opposition.
The office of Hong Kong Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa unveiled a diluted version of restrictions on demonstrations and a modified ban on foreign funding of local political groups.

Tung said later changes were made after digesting over 5,500 written views canvassed during a three-week public consultation exercise marked by strong opposition from the pro-democracy camp to any rollback of political freedoms and rights.
"We have listened carefully to public opinions on the consulatation document and have taken positive steps to address some of the concerns expressed," he said in a speech to the Asia Society.
"I want to assure you that I am firmly committed to safeguarding the rights of the indivudual and freedoms of the individual of Hong Kong which we currently enjoy."
But opponents said the future government remained deaf to their fears and argued that the plans were unchanged on essentials.

The Democratic Party said Tung was paying mere lip service to the consultation exercise. "They have not given way at all. Larger principles have not changed," said party vice-chairman and elected legislator Yeung Sum.
"What we can see is his loyalty to what China wants," said legislator Albert Ho, a Democractic Party member.
Outgoing British Governor Chris Patten said Tung's office had failed again to explain why any curbs were needed.

"The central question that people have been asking about this exercise remains unanswered, and that is why any of it should be necessary," he said, adding that present laws worked well and public order in Hong Kong was as good as anywhere.

Ho and his Democratic Party collegues will be forced out of their legislative roles on July 1, when the elected Legislative Council is replaced by the Provisional Legislature, a body chosen by a China-backed selection committee.

Lower-tier councils will apparently remain intact under the proposals announced by Tung's office. But the Urban and Regional Councils and the 18 District Boards will be expanded by 25 percent with new, appointed members.

"The bills provide for a seamless transition," a Tung spokesman said. "At the same time, the bills enable these new district organisations to benefit from further professional input through the appointment of additional members."
Despite ongoing friction in the political arena, there were signs that confidence in Hong Kong's prospects remained high.

A survey of 196 members by the British Chamber of Commerce in the territory showed an overall air of confidence in the future, although fears of rising corruption and declining English language standards clouded the picture.
The government said Japan had agreed to give holders of the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region passports the same treatment as holders of Hong Kong British travel documents.
Easy access to major travel destinations is seen as essential for the territory's business prospects and a barometer of international confidence in Hong Kong beyond the handover.

With the transition now just 47 days away, more signs emerged of the rush to finish preparations. Beijing issued a conditional invitation to representatives from political arch-rival Taiwan to attend the ceremony marking the handover.

And the government invited bids for 27 old Royal Mail pillar boxes -- bright red, cast iron mail boxes complete with the British crown insignia and royal monogram. Royal symbols are being purged from the territory in the runup to June 30.
